text.en: A plant has no stove, yet it makes its own food. Its leaves are tiny kitchens that use sunlight. We learn how plants make food, take in water and breathe.

Photosynthesis is how green plants make food. Leaves take in carbon dioxide from air through tiny pores called stomata, and roots take in water. Chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, captures sunlight. Using the light, the plant turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and releases oxygen. Plants use some of the sugar they make and can store some as starch. They are called producers because they make their own food.
Roots take water and minerals from the soil. Xylem tubes carry water upward to the leaves. Phloem tubes carry food from leaves to other parts.
Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the leaves through stomata. It cools the plant and pulls water up from the roots.
Plants also respire: they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide, day and night. Some plants, like insect-eating pitcher plants, get extra nutrients from insects.

A plant grows when it makes new tissue, such as longer roots or new leaves. Measure it over several days to see a lasting change.
To compare heights, start each reading at the soil surface and use the same ruler and units.
Two seedlings of the same kind make a more useful comparison than two unrelated plants.
If you are testing light, give both seedlings similar water, pots and soil. Otherwise their difference could be caused by something else.

board.text: Change one condition at a time

text.en: A green leaf uses light as an energy source. Water and carbon dioxide provide the material that becomes sugar.

board.text: Energy from light, materials from air and water

text.en: Chlorophyll absorbs some of the light reaching the leaf. It helps the leaf use that energy to make sugar.
A leaf can change some of its sugar into starch for storage. Finding starch can give a clue about where food was made.
Imagine the same leaf with one part covered and one part exposed to light. Comparing the two parts helps test the role of light.

board.text: Compare covered and lit leaf patches

text.en: If only the exposed leaf patch shows starch afterward, that supports the idea that light was needed to make and store the food.

board.text: Evidence: starch in the lit patch

text.en: Use parts of the same leaf or similar leaves. This way the amount of light is the main difference you are testing.
Compare starch in green and pale patches of a leaf exposed to light. Finding starch in the green patches supports a role for chlorophyll.
A stoma is a tiny opening. Stomata let gases, such as carbon dioxide and oxygen, move between the leaf and the surrounding air.

board.text: Stomata are pores in the leaf surface

text.en: Roots take up water and dissolved minerals. The sugar used by much of the plant is made in green tissues.
As water travels upward, it carries dissolved minerals through xylem. At the leaf, some of the water can be used to make food.
In a classroom model, a stem put in coloured water can show colour higher up. This is evidence that water moves through the stem.
Sugars can move in phloem from a leaf towards places where they are needed, such as a young shoot, a fruit or a storage root.

board.text: Phloem: leaves → growing or storage parts

text.en: Xylem takes water and minerals mainly upward. Phloem carries sugar from areas that supply it to areas that use or store it.
Water vapour can leave through stomata. This movement helps draw replacement water up the plant.

board.text: Water vapour can escape from leaves

text.en: Plant cells use oxygen to release energy from sugars. That energy helps them grow and carry out other jobs.
In enough light, a leaf can photosynthesise and respire together. The two processes do different jobs.
Without enough light, photosynthesis stops. Living cells still respire and use their supply of sugar.
A seed that has started growing can use stored food for energy, even before its first green leaf makes sugar.
Trace water from the soil to a leaf through xylem. Then trace sugar from the leaf to a growing bud through phloem.

board.text: Follow the materials from source to use

problem.en: What does a plant need to make food?

text.en: Sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and chlorophyll.
It gives out oxygen.

problem.en: Two areas of one leaf received different amounts of light. Starch was found only in the lit area. What does this show?

text.en: The two areas were parts of the same leaf.

why.en: Their amounts of light differed while most other conditions matched.

text.en: The result supports a role for light in making starch.

why.en: The comparison connects the observation to the condition changed.

problem.en: A root supplies water and a green leaf supplies sugars. How does each move to a growing shoot?

text.en: Water travels from the roots in xylem.

why.en: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward.

text.en: Sugars made in the leaf travel in phloem.

why.en: The growing shoot can use them for energy and new material.

prompt.en: Explain why plants are important for animals.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking plants breathe only at night.

points.en: Xylem carries water; phloem carries food.
